claim: Childhood maltreatment (CM) increases the risk for the development of multiple psychopathologies and medical conditions over the lifespan.
source: Exposure to CM increases the risk for the development of multiple psychopathologies and medical conditions over the lifespan (Anda et al., 2006; Nemeroff, 2016; Teicher and Samson, 2016; Kaffman and Meaney, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Anda et al., 2006; Nemeroff, 2016; Teicher and Samson, 2016; Kaffman and Meaney, 2007)

claim: The estimated annual economic burden of childhood maltreatment is $2 trillion in the United States alone.
source: with an estimated annual economic burden of $2 trillion in the United States alone (Peterson et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peterson et al., 2018

claim: 30–40% of the adult population have experienced some form of childhood maltreatment.
source: Given that 30–40% of the adult population have experienced some form of CM (Agorastos et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Agorastos et al., 2019

claim: The risk of negative outcomes raises linearly with the number of maltreatment exposures according to the cumulative risk perspective.
source: The study of CM-associated outcomes is generally framed from a cumulative risk perspective, where the risk of negative outcomes raises linearly with the number of maltreatment exposures (Kessler et al., 1997; Anda et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2010; Evans et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Kessler et al., 1997; Anda et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2010; Evans et al., 2013)

claim: Different forms of childhood maltreatment fall along multiple dimensions, which more directly impacts later outcomes than number of CM instances per se.
source: Newer models have expanded this framework to highlight that different forms of CM fall along multiple dimensions, and this in turn more directly impacts later outcomes than number of CM instances per se (McLaughlin et al., 2014; McLaughlin and Sheridan, 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McLaughlin et al., 2014 and McLaughlin and Sheridan, 2016

claim: Neither cumulative risk models nor dimensional models have addressed the potential role that sex plays in moderating CM-associated outcomes.
source: However, neither of these models has addressed the potential role that sex plays in moderating CM-associated outcomes (Bath, 2020; White and Kaffman, 2019b)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bath, 2020 and White and Kaffman, 2019b

claim: Similar clinical presentation may be driven by different underlying mechanisms in males and females as reported for depression.
source: Importantly, similar clinical presentation may be driven by different underlying mechanisms in males and females as reported for depression (Labonté et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Labonté et al., 2017

claim: Similar clinical presentation may be driven by different underlying mechanisms in males and females as reported for neuropathic pain.
source: similar clinical presentation may be driven by different underlying mechanisms in males and females as reported for depression (Labonté et al., 2017) and neuropathic pain (Sorge et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sorge et al., 2015

claim: Sex-specific interventions might be needed to more effectively treat psychiatric and medical consequences of childhood maltreatment.
source: These findings suggest that sex-specific interventions might be needed to more effectively treat psychiatric and medical consequences of CM (Bath, 2020; White and Kaffman, 2019b)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bath, 2020 and White and Kaffman, 2019b, and is based on inference from previous findings about sex-specific mechanisms

claim: Structural MRI studies show reduced hippocampal and corpus callosum volume in those exposed to childhood maltreatment.
source: The most reproducible findings are from structural MRI studies which show reduced hippocampal and corpus callosum volume in those exposed to CM, with a hint that these effects are larger in males compared to age-matched females (Teicher and Samson, 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Teicher and Samson, 2016

claim: A recent multi-center study using a large cohort of 3036 individuals did not find any significant changes in hippocampal size but noted reduced caudate size in females that was not seen in males exposed to childhood maltreatment.
source: A recent multi-center study using a large cohort of 3036 individuals did not find any significant changes in hippocampal size but noted reduced caudate size in females that was not seen in males exposed to CM (Frodl et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Frodl et al., 2017

claim: The vast majority of early life stress work in rodents and non-human primates has been done only in males.
source: Although rodents and non-human primates exposed to early life stress (ELS) show similar behavioral and physiological outcomes reported in human studies, the vast majority of work has been done only in males (White and Kaffman, 2019b; Bath, 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to White and Kaffman, 2019b and Bath, 2020

claim: The few studies that used imaging to characterize outcomes in rodent models of early life stress were done exclusively in males.
source: Specifically, the few studies that used imaging to characterize outcomes in rodent models of ELS were done exclusively in males (Bolton et al., 2018; Molet et al., 2016; Carlyle et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2017; Guadagno et al., 2018a; Sarabdjitsingh et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2018), with only one imaging study examining outcomes in both sexes (Honeycutt et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Bolton et al., 2018; Molet et al., 2016; Carlyle et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2017; Guadagno et al., 2018a; Sarabdjitsingh et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2018)

claim: Only one imaging study examining early life stress outcomes in rodents examined outcomes in both sexes.
source: with only one imaging study examining outcomes in both sexes (Honeycutt et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Honeycutt et al., 2020

claim: There are considerable neuroanatomical sex differences in the postnatal mouse brain.
source: The need to extend these findings to females is highlighted by a report of considerable neuroanatomical sex differences in the postnatal mouse brain (Qiu et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Qiu et al., 2018

claim: Maternal separation leads to sex-specific effects in amygdala connectivity with the prefrontal cortex in adolescent rats.
source: and a recent study showing that maternal separation leads to sex-specific effects in amygdala (AMY) connectivity with the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in adolescent rats (Honeycutt et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Honeycutt et al., 2020

claim: The unpredictable postnatal stress (UPS) paradigm was modified and built upon the widely used limited bedding and nesting (LBN) paradigm developed by Tallie Baram's lab.
source: Our lab has modified and built upon the widely used limited bedding and nesting (LBN) paradigm developed by Tallie Baram's lab (Walker et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2017

claim: The UPS paradigm extends the time frame dam and pups are exposed to LBN from PND2-9 to PND0-25.
source: by extending the time frame dam and pups are exposed to LBN (from PND2-9 to PND0-25)
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text describing the UPS paradigm modifications

claim: The UPS paradigm adds brief, 1 hr, bouts of maternal separation on an unpredictable schedule (PND 14, 16, 17, 21, 22, and 25), followed by nest disruption.
source: and adding brief, 1 hr, bouts of maternal separation on an unpredictable schedule, that is, PND 14, 16, 17, 21, 22, and 25, followed by nest disruption
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text describing the UPS paradigm modifications

claim: Balb/cByj mice were used due to their high sensitivity to stress.
source: Balb/cByj mice were used due to their high sensitivity to stress (Caldji et al., 2004; Zaharia et al., 1996; Francis et al., 2003; Carola et al., 2004; Tractenberg et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2010; Wei et al., 2012; McWhirt et al., 2019; Malki et al., 2015; Flint and Tinkle, 2001; Wei et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2015; Delpech et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting stress sensitivity in Balb/cByj mice

claim: Balb/cByj dams can reliably maintain their litters in the complete absence of nesting material.
source: and the ability of Balb/cByj dams to reliably maintain their litters in the complete absence of nesting material (Wei et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2010

claim: UPS produces an elevated anxiety phenotype in both adolescent and adult Balb/cByj offspring.
source: Further, we have previously shown that UPS produces an elevated anxiety phenotype in both adolescent and adult Balb/cByj offspring (Johnson et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Johnson et al., 2018

claim: Using rsfMRI, increased fronto-limbic connectivity was found in UPS male mice that included increased AMY–PFC and AMY–hippocampus connectivity.
source: Using rsfMRI we found increased fronto-limbic connectivity in UPS male mice that included increased AMY–PFC and AMY–hippocampus connectivity, the strength of which was highly correlated with anxiety-like behaviors (Johnson et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Johnson et al., 2018

claim: The strength of fronto-limbic connectivity in UPS male mice was highly correlated with anxiety-like behaviors.
source: Using rsfMRI we found increased fronto-limbic connectivity in UPS male mice that included increased AMY–PFC and AMY–hippocampus connectivity, the strength of which was highly correlated with anxiety-like behaviors (Johnson et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Johnson et al., 2018

claim: Females did not show an elevated anxiety phenotype in response to UPS.
source: Interestingly, females did not show an elevated anxiety phenotype, suggesting that UPS may affect males and females differently
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the study

claim: UPS may affect males and females differently.
source: Interestingly, females did not show an elevated anxiety phenotype, suggesting that UPS may affect males and females differently
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that females did not show an elevated anxiety phenotype

claim: UPS animals were significantly smaller than control animals at P14.
source: A main effect of rearing on body weight was consistently found at P14 (F (1, 106)=36.66, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.257 Figure 1A and B) and P26 (F (1, 104)=61.22, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.303, Figure 1C) showing that UPS animals were significantly smaller than control (CTL) animals
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F (1, 106)=36.66, p<0.001) and reference to Figure 1A and B

claim: UPS animals were significantly smaller than control animals at P26.
source: A main effect of rearing on body weight was consistently found at P14 (F (1, 106)=36.66, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.257 Figure 1A and B) and P26 (F (1, 104)=61.22, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.303, Figure 1C) showing that UPS animals were significantly smaller than control (CTL) animals
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F (1, 104)=61.22, p<0.001) and reference to Figure 1C

claim: No significant effects of sex or an interaction were seen in 14- and 26-day-old pups for body weight.
source: No significant effects of sex or an interaction were seen in 14- and 26-day-old pups (p>0.05)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p>0.05)

claim: The effect of rearing on body weight persisted into adulthood.
source: The effect of rearing persisted into adulthood (F (1, 28)=7.86, p=0.009 ηp2 = 0.219, Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F (1, 28)=7.86, p=0.009) and reference to Figure 1D

claim: There was a significant main effect of sex on adult body weight.
source: with a significant main effect of sex (F (1, 28)=80.31, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.741)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F (1, 28)=80.31, p<0.0001)

claim: There was no interaction between sex and rearing on adult body weight.
source: but no interaction between sex and rearing (F (1, 28)=0.03, p=0.87, ηp2 = 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F (1, 28)=0.03, p=0.87)

claim: There was a significant interaction of sex and rearing on corticosterone level.

evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F (1, 25)=9.37, p=0.005)

claim: UPS males showed a significant reduction in corticosterone levels compared to control males.

claim: UPS females did not show a significant reduction in corticosterone levels compared to control females.
source: Sidak's post-hoc analysis revealed a significant reduction in corticosterone levels in UPS compared to CTL males (p=0.01, Cohn's d = −1.4), which was not seen in females (p=0.31, Cohn's d = 0.9, Figure 1E)

claim: There was a significant main effect of sex on corticosterone levels.

claim: There was no main effect of rearing on corticosterone levels.

claim: There was a significant effect of sex on normalized adrenal gland weight, with females having greater weight than males.

claim: There were no significant effects of sex, rearing, or an interaction on time spent in the center of the open field.
source: Two-way ANOVA revealed no significant effects of sex, rearing, or an interaction on time spent in the center of the open field (sex: F (1, 68)=1.34, p=0.25, ηp2 = 0.019; rearing: F (1, 68)=0.912, p=0.34, ηp2 = 0.013; interaction: F (1, 68)=3.37, p=0.31, ηp2 = 0.015; Figure 2A)

claim: There were no significant effects of sex, rearing, or an interaction on total distance traveled in the open field.

evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2B

claim: UPS-reared animals spent significantly more time in the open arms of the elevated plus maze.

evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F (1, 72)=7.411, p=0.008) and reference to Figure 2C

claim: There were no significant effects of sex or interaction on time spent in open arms of the EPM.

evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis

claim: There were no differences in closed arm exploration in the EPM.

evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2D

claim: UPS mice spent significantly less time exploring novel objects.

claim: The effect of sex on time exploring novel objects was not replicated in the additional cohort.

claim: There were no inherent differences in baseline freezing activity between sexes or rearing conditions prior to the onset of shocks.

evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis from an additional cohort

claim: Animals froze more as the number of shocks experienced increased regardless of sex or rearing condition.
source: Repeated measures ANOVA revealed a significant effect of freezing behavior over time (Greenhouse–Geisser: F (2.2686, 272)=91.38, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.573; cohort 2: F (2.464, 248)=70.50, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.532) where animals froze more as the number of shocks experienced increased regardless of sex or rearing condition
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis from repeated measures ANOVA

claim: UPS-reared animals froze significantly less to the original training context compared to control-reared counterparts.
source: Two-way ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of rearing (F (1, 68)=18.52, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.214; Figure 2F) where UPS-reared animals froze significantly less to the original training context compared to CTL-reared counterparts
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F (1, 68)=18.52, p<0.001) and reference to Figure 2F

claim: The effect of UPS on reduced contextual freezing was replicated in cohort 2.
source: an effect that was replicated in cohort 2 (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to data in Supplementary file 1

claim: There were no significant effects of sex or an interaction on contextual freezing in cohort 1.

evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis

claim: The UPS rearing condition leads to reproducible deficits in context encoding or retrieval.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the UPS rearing condition leads to reproducible deficits in context encoding or retrieval
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed deficits in contextual freezing across cohorts

claim: Tone exposure produced significantly higher freezing behavior indicating appropriate cue-mediated learning.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: There were no consistent effects of rearing, sex, or interaction on baseline freezing and responses to tone-on and tone-off episodes.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: There was a significant main effect of sex on cue-recall, with females freezing more than males to the cue.

evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F (1, 68)=8.57, p=0.005) and reference to Figure 2G

claim: The effect of sex on cue-induced freezing was replicated in cohort 2.
source: an effect replicated in cohort 2 (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to data in Supplementary file 1

claim: There were no significant effects of rearing condition or an interaction on cue-induced freezing.

claim: Behavioral outcomes in novel exploration test and contextual fear conditioning are not likely to be mediated by a litter effect.

evidence: The claim is supported by linear mixed-effect analyses shown in Supplementary file 2

claim: UPS mice showed increased volumes in the nucleus accumbens, olfactory bulb, cingulate cortex, subregions within the sensory cortex, ventral hippocampus, and amygdala.

evidence: The claim is supported by voxel-based morphometric analysis data

claim: UPS mice showed reduced volumes in the frontal cortex, PFC, subregions of the motor cortex, the sensory cortex, fimbria, striatum, and thalamus.

claim: Males showed increased volumes in subregions of the BNST, medial preoptic area, olfactory bulb, and dorsal hippocampus compared to females.

evidence: The claim is supported by voxel-based morphometric analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Males showed reduced volume in parts of the motor cortex, sensory cortex, striatum, and thalamus compared to females.
source: Using these parameters, males showed increased volumes in subregions of the BNST, medial preoptic area, OB, and dorsal hippocampus (dHC) and reduced volume in parts of the MO, sensory cortex, striatum, and thalamus when compared to the female mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by voxel-based morphometric analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: No brain regions showed UPS by sex interaction after correcting for multiple comparisons and adjusting the minimal cluster size to more than 20.
source: No brain regions showed UPS by sex interaction after correcting for multiple comparisons and adjusting the minimal cluster size to more than 20

claim: Increased FA in UPS was most pronounced in subregions of the sensory cortex, hypothalamus, and amygdala.

claim: Reduced FA in UPS was seen in the rostral corpus callosum and stria medularis.
source: Increased FA in UPS was most pronounced in subregions of the sensory cortex, hypothalamus, and AMY with reduced FA was seen in the rostral corpus callosum and stria medularis (Figure 4)
evidence: The claim is supported by FA analysis data shown in Figure 4

claim: The dMRI projections show good agreement with the expected anterograde connectivity available from the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas.

evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: There was a significant interaction between sex and rearing on the number of streamlines between the AMY and the PFC.

claim: There was a significant effect of sex within the UPS condition for AMY-PFC connectivity, but not the control condition.

claim: There was a significant effect of rearing condition on AMY-PFC connectivity for males, but not for females.

claim: AMY–PFC connectivity was significantly increased in UPS-reared males but was not altered in UPS-reared females.

claim: There was a significant effect of rearing and interaction between rearing and sex on the number of streamlines between the vHC and the PFC.

evidence: The claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis

claim: There was a significant effect of rearing condition on vHC-PFC connectivity for males, but not females.

claim: vHC–PFC showed a similar pattern of connectivity to that seen between the AMY and the PFC, with UPS increasing the number of streamline projections in males but not females.

claim: The left hemisphere showed significantly higher AMY-hippocampus connectivity compared to the right hemisphere.
